theory.intro: A **representative** sample reflects important features of its target population. Check who can be selected, who responds, the sample size and the shares of relevant groups. A fair method helps, but does not guarantee an exact result.
facts: An incomplete selection list leaves out part of the target population. Random selection from that list cannot include the missing people.
**Convenience bias** occurs when choosing easily reached people over-represents that specific group and excludes others.
**Volunteer bias** may occur when people choose whether to respond. Those who reply may have different views from those who do not.
A very **small sample** may miss the variety in the population. A few unusual replies can greatly change its result.
**Proportional stratified sampling** chooses randomly within relevant groups and matches their population shares. This helps representation; matching one feature does not guarantee all views match.
A **simple random sample** from a complete population list gives every member an equal chance of selection.

workedExamples.question_text:
A council wants the views of all adult residents about public transport.
(a) It interviews people at the main bus stop on Monday morning. Explain the coverage problem and suggest a fairer selection.
(b) It instead reports 2400 replies to a link on its website. Explain why the larger number does not settle the problem.
workedExamples.solution_text:
(a) Residents who do not use that bus stop at that time cannot be selected. Their travel needs may differ from those of the people interviewed.
Choose different residents at random from a complete list of the target population, and provide suitable ways for selected people to answer.
(b) Only people who see the link and choose to reply are included. Their views may differ from those of other residents. More voluntary replies do not remove restricted coverage or volunteer bias.

workedExamples.question_text:
Two surveys choose residents at random from the same complete list. Everyone selected answers. Survey A chooses 3 residents and Survey B chooses 69.
(a) Explain why A is a weak basis for representing the community.
(b) Why is B preferable, and what does it still not guarantee?
workedExamples.solution_text:
(a) Three residents may miss much of the variety in the community. One unusual reply can greatly change the result.
(b) B uses the same fair method with more residents, so a few unusual replies have less influence and more variety may be included. It does not guarantee that the sample views exactly match the views of the whole community.

workedExamples.question_text:
A library has $420$, $660$ and $360$ borrowers at three branches. It wants a proportional sample of $72$.
(a) Find how many to choose from each branch.
(b) A proposed sample has $16$, $37$ and $19$ borrowers respectively. Compare it with the proportional numbers and identify the most over-represented branch.
workedExamples.solution_text:
(a) Total $=420+660+360=1440$.
The sample share is $\frac{72}{1440}=\frac1{20}$.
First branch: $420\div20=21$.
Second branch: $660\div20=33$.
Third branch: $360\div20=18$.
$21+33+18=72$. Choose these numbers at random within the branches.
(b) The first branch has $16$, which is $5$ fewer than $21$.
The second has $37$, which is $4$ more than $33$.
The third has $19$, which is $1$ more than $18$.
The second branch is the most over-represented. The proposed sample totals $72$, but its branch shares do not match the population.

workedExamples.question_text: A staff list repeats six entries: one night-shift worker followed by five day-shift workers. A survey takes positions 1, 7, 13, 19 and so on. Explain why this systematic selection is a problem and suggest a fairer method.
workedExamples.solution_text:
The step is 6, the same as the repeating pattern. Every selected position is the night-shift worker in that block. Day-shift workers cannot be selected, and their views may differ.
Choose different names at random from the complete staff list instead. Simply increasing the number selected by the same repeating step does not fix the exclusion.

foundation.question_text:
A researcher investigates the average weekly exercise hours of all adults in a town by surveying people exiting a gymnasium on Saturday morning.
Decide whether the sample is representative and name the over-represented group.
foundation.solution_text:
Gym users are over-represented, while adults who do not attend this gym at that time cannot be selected. Exercise habits of gym users may differ from those of other adults.
The selection does not fairly represent all adults in the town.

foundation.question_text:
A radio host asks listeners to text in whether they support higher tolls on the harbour bridge.
$1500$ listeners text in.
Decide whether the sample is representative and justify your answer.
foundation.solution_text:
Only listeners who choose to text are included. Their views may differ from other listeners and from people who do not listen to the station.
The 1500 replies do not remove self-selection or the restricted coverage.

foundation.question_text:
To estimate the proportion of voters in a state of $4\,000\,000$ people who support a new policy, a pollster randomly selects $5$ voters.
Decide whether this sample is representative and justify your answer.
foundation.solution_text:
Five randomly chosen voters may miss much of the variety in the population. Changing one reply changes the sample percentage by $\frac15\times100\%=20\%$.
This is a weak basis for representing the state's voters, even though selection is random.

foundation.question_text:
A high school has $800$ students.
The principal assigns every student a number from $1$ to $800$ and uses a computer random number generator to select $100$ students for a survey on school facilities.
Decide whether this sample is representative and justify your answer.
foundation.solution_text:
Selecting different students at random from the complete roll gives every student an equal chance of selection.
This is a fair way to choose a sample of the school. It avoids systematic exclusions, but the sample may still differ from the population by chance.

foundation.question_text:
A university has $6000$ undergraduate students and $2000$ postgraduate students (total $8000$).
A researcher takes a sample of $200$ undergraduates and $200$ postgraduates.
Determine whether this sample is representative of the student body and justify your answer.
foundation.solution_text:
Undergraduates make up $75\%$ of the population but only $50\%$ of the sample, while postgraduates are over-represented.
Not representative; the strata are sampled in equal numbers rather than in proportion to population size.

foundation.question_text:
A survey aims to determine the reading habits of all residents in a city by interviewing people at the central city library on a weekday afternoon.
Identify which subgroup is under-represented.
foundation.solution_text:
Residents who do not use the library at that time cannot be selected. This may under-represent people at work or school then and people who rarely use the library.
Their reading habits may differ, so this location and time do not fairly cover all residents.

foundation.question_text:
A company has $400$ full-time staff and $100$ part-time staff (total $500$).
A sample of $50$ staff contains $40$ full-time and $10$ part-time staff.
Determine whether the sample is representative regarding employment type.
foundation.solution_text:
Full-time: $\frac{400}{500}=80\%$ of population, $\frac{40}{50}=80\%$ of sample.
Part-time: $\frac{100}{500}=20\%$ of population, $\frac{10}{50}=20\%$ of sample.
Representative; the sample proportions exactly match the population proportions.

development.question_text:
A political polling organisation wants to survey voting intentions in an upcoming federal election.
They conduct phone interviews using landline numbers listed in the White Pages.
Explain why this sampling frame produces an unrepresentative sample.
development.solution_text:
The landline directory leaves out voters without listed landlines, including mobile-only households. Their views may differ from those of listed landline users.
Random selection within the directory cannot include the missing voters.

development.question_text:
A high school has the following enrolment numbers by year group:
$\begin{array}{lcccccc}\textbf{Year}&7&8&9&10&11&12\\ \hline \textbf{Students}&150&150&150&150&200&200\end{array}$
A survey on homework policy selects $20$ students from each of the $6$ year groups (total $120$).
Explain why this sample does not represent the student population accurately.
development.solution_text:
Total population $=1000$ students. Year 11 and 12 make up $20\%$ each (should be 24 students each in a sample of 120), but only receive 20.
Years 7 to 10 make up $15\%$ each (should be 18 students each), but receive 20.
Not representative; senior students are under-represented relative to junior students.

development.question_text:
An online shopping platform emails a customer satisfaction survey to all $50\,000$ customers who made a purchase last month.
$800$ customers complete the survey.
The company claims the sample represents all customers because every customer received the email.
Evaluate this claim.
development.solution_text:
Inviting everyone does not mean everyone is included in the responses. Only 800 of the 50,000 invited customers chose to answer; their experiences may differ from those who did not reply.
The invitation list alone does not establish that the responses represent all customers.

development.question_text:
A regional council manages $12\,000$ rateable properties.
Using the official rates register, the council selects every $40$th property after generating a random starting integer between $1$ and $40$, achieving a sample of $300$ properties.
Evaluate whether this sample is representative.
development.solution_text:
The complete rates register and random start give every property an equal chance of selection.
This is a fair design if the list has no repeating pattern that matches the step of 40. Check that possible problem before relying on the sample; neither a random start nor 300 selections guarantees an exact result.

development.question_text:
A dental clinic wants to know how satisfied local residents are with local healthcare.
The clinic distributes questionnaires to patients sitting in its waiting room.
Identify the selection mechanism causing bias and state the effect on the survey conclusion.
development.solution_text:
Only people attending this dental clinic at that time can be selected. Residents who use other services or cannot access this clinic are missed.
The patients' views may differ from those of other residents, so the sample does not fairly cover the local population. The information given does not show whether satisfaction would be overestimated or underestimated.

development.question_text:
A factory produces $500\,000$ microchips daily.
Quality control tests $10$ microchips chosen at random across the day and finds $0$ defects, concluding the entire daily batch has a $0\%$ defect rate.
Explain why this conclusion is unjustified.
development.solution_text:
Only $10$ chips are tested, which is $\frac{10}{500000}\times100\%=0.002\%$ of the batch.
The untested chips may include defects even though none of these ten chips were defective.
A tiny sample with no defects does not establish a $0\%$ defect rate for the whole batch.

development.question_text:
A hospital employs $300$ doctors, $600$ nurses, and $100$ administrative staff (total $1000$).
A proposed representative sample of $100$ staff consists of $30$ doctors, $60$ nurses, and $10$ administrative staff.
Verify mathematically whether this sample is representative by role.
development.solution_text:
Population ratios: Doctors $30\%$, Nurses $60\%$, Admin $10\%$.
Sample counts: Doctors $30$ ($30\%$), Nurses $60$ ($60\%$), Admin $10$ ($10\%$).
$\frac{30}{100}=0.30$, $\frac{60}{100}=0.60$, $\frac{10}{100}=0.10$.
Representative; each professional group is sampled in exact proportion to its size in the hospital population.

mastery.question_text:
A social media influencer with $1\,000\,000$ followers runs a poll on their profile asking: 'Do you believe university degrees are worth the tuition cost?' $120\,000$ followers vote, with $85\%$ voting 'No'.
The influencer asserts that $85\%$ of young Australians reject university degrees.
Justify why this massive sample remains unrepresentative of young Australians.
mastery.solution_text:
1. Followers of this influencer do not cover all young Australians; their views and experiences may differ.
2. Only followers who choose to vote are included, so volunteer bias is possible.
3. More replies do not remove either of these selection problems. The 85% describes the 120,000 respondents, not necessarily all young Australians.

mastery.question_text:
A national sports league has $320$ players across four divisions: Division 1 ($160$ players), Division 2 ($80$ players), Division 3 ($48$ players), and Division 4 ($32$ players).
An athlete welfare committee selects a sample of $40$ players containing $14$ from Division 1, $12$ from Division 2, $9$ from Division 3, and $5$ from Division 4.
Calculate the required proportional quota for each division, compare with the actual sample, and identify which division is most over-represented.
mastery.solution_text:
Sample fraction: $\frac{40}{320}=\frac{1}{8}$.
Required quotas: Division 1: $\frac{160}{8}=20$; Division 2: $\frac{80}{8}=10$; Division 3: $\frac{48}{8}=6$; Division 4: $\frac{32}{8}=4$.
Actual sample: Division 1 has $14$ (under by $6$), Division 2 has $12$ (over by $2$), Division 3 has $9$ (over by $3$), Division 4 has $5$ (over by $1$).
Not representative; Division 3 is the most over-represented division (over by $3$ players, or $+50\%$ above its quota).

mastery.question_text:
A council wishes to determine the attitudes of enrolled adult voters toward a proposed new park.
It uses the complete municipal electoral roll and a stratified sampling plan by age group (18–34, 35–54, 55+) matching the proportions on that roll.
Selected voters are contacted by mail and phone with multiple follow-ups, achieving an $85\%$ response rate.
Give two features of the design that help the sample represent this target population.
mastery.solution_text:
1. The complete electoral roll covers the stated target population of enrolled adult voters; it does not cover every resident.
2. Matching age-group proportions helps represent those groups. Mail and phone follow-ups also encourage selected voters to reply.
Check the age shares of the actual responses: the 15% who did not respond may have different views, so the design does not guarantee perfect representation.
